title: CAG-WM: A Synthetic-Data-Driven Coronary World Model for Autonomous Guidewire Navigation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Well motivated problem with clear clinical relevance:The paper tackles autonomous coronary guidewire navigation, a high impact and technically challenging task in PCI that involves long horizon planning under partial observability. 2.Novel integration of synthetic data, physics simulation, and world models:A key contribution is the coherent integration of synthetic angiography 3D data generation, SOFA-based physical simulation, and a TD-MPC2-based world model into a unified training pipeline. While each component exists individually, combining them to form a closed loop system for learning guidewire vessel dynamics is original and practically valuable, especially for data scarce medical robotics tasks. 3.Demonstrated effectiveness on real clinical data despite synthetic training:The method is trained entirely on synthetic data yet shows clear performance gains over RL and existing world model baselines on multi center clinical datasets. This suggests that the approach has promising generalization ability and provides an encouraging step toward real world deployment in endovascular intervention tasks.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Limited analysis of synthetic-to-real generalization:While the method is trained on synthetic data and evaluated on real clinical cases, the paper provides limited analysis of the domain gap between synthetic and real angiography. For instance, it would strengthen the work to include additional studies on how differences in imaging characteristics or anatomical variability affect performance. Prior sim-to-real studies often include such analyses or adaptation strategies, and incorporating similar evaluations here could further support the claimed generalization ability. 2.Methodological novelty is primarily at the system level:The proposed approach builds upon existing world model frameworks, particularly TD-MPC2 , with task specific adaptations in observation design and reward formulation. While this integration is well-motivated and effective for the application, the methodological contribution is mainly at the system and application level rather than introducing a fundamentally new world model formulation. Clarifying this positioning could help better align expectations regarding novelty. 3.Clarity and fairness of baseline comparisons could be improved:The proposed method leverages structured inputs such as guidewire points, vessel centerlines, and target locations (Sec. 2.3) . It is not entirely clear whether all baselines are provided with the same input representations, or whether some operate on different modalities. Providing additional clarification or controlled comparisons with consistent observation spaces would make the performance gains more directly attributable to the proposed modeling approach.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: (1) Technical novelty and innovation: Applying a world model to coronary guidewire navigation is a relevant and reasonably novel direction. The integration of synthetic full-view CAG, reconstructed 3D anatomy, and SOFA-based physical simulation is a meaningful systems contribution. Figures 1 and 2 present the high-level workflow clearly. (2) Experimental rigor and validation: The paper evaluates against three classes of baselines: model-free RL, planning-based methods, and world-model-based methods. It reports three metrics on two test sources (InCAG and VMR), and includes a reward ablation study. At a minimum, the experimental surface is broader than many papers in this area. Tables 1 and 2 attempt to characterize performance, failure quality, and runtime. (3) Clarity of presentation: The manuscript is generally well organized. The problem setup, framework overview, experimental protocol, and result sections are easy to follow. Figure 1 provides a useful system overview, and Figure 3 offers qualitative visualizations of navigation trajectories and training-space coverage.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: (1) The main concern is that the algorithmic novelty appears limited. The core seems closer to “TD-MPC2 + task-specific observation engineering + reward design + synthetic simulation environment” than to a substantially new world-model formulation. The paper claims “the first synthetic-data-driven world model,” but the actual methodological advance over TD-MPC2 is not sharply defined. For a top-tier venue, the manuscript needs to separate system integration novelty from algorithmic novelty much more clearly. (2) The manuscript repeatedly claims the method is end-to-end from angiographic observations to actions, but Sec. 2.3 explicitly states that it first detects the stenosis target, tracks guidewire points, and extracts vessel centerlines before encoding them with TCNs and an MLP. Sec. 3.1 further states that all perceptual information required by the observation is pre-extracted prior to training. This is not a standard end-to-end setup; it is a staged pipeline with substantial structured intermediate supervision. The wording is therefore misleading. (3) The mathematical and physical descriptions are under-specified. Eq. (2) is not explained in enough detail for reproducibility, and the dynamic vessel-wall deformation model is especially unclear. The manuscript claims dynamic vascular properties, but it does not establish whether the displacement field reflects realistic cardiac/respiratory motion or merely synthetic perturbations. At present, the dynamic environment seems plausible as a simulation device, but not yet clinically validated.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Practical data generation strategy: [2] produces what I consider the most realistic synthetic coronary angiography (XA/DSA) images to date, built upon EG3D[1], though [2] only applies this capability to translational correction for PCI camera calibration. The present work directly inherits this generation pipeline from [2] and repurposes it for supporting simulation environments for guidewire navigation training. While the generation module itself is not new, I view this as a valuable contribution: the gap between synthetic training data and transferable navigation policies has been repeatedly identified as a bottleneck in prior literature [7,8], yet no prior work has offered a convincing solution. That said, I note with some puzzlement that although the pipeline produces highly realistic 2D angiographic images, the method does not directly consume these images. Instead, it extracts intermediate representations (point coordinates, centerlines) and discards the visual realism. This appears to leave the most distinctive advantage of the generation pipeline underutilized, and I would appreciate the authors’ clarification on this design choice or correct my misunderstanding (I have to say the method and experiment part is too confusing, and some parts seem to be blurred. :-) ) . Open codebase: I carefully went through the codebase, and confirmed that the codebase contains the full SOFA-based CAG-EVE environment plus the TD-MPC2 training/evaluation scripts, but the perception/data-generation pieces described in the paper (EG3D angiography synthesis, guidewire/centerline detectors, and the 20-case clinical geometry set) are missing, which prevents end-to-end reproduction of the reported “from angiography” results. Graphical content: Figures are high quality and well designed. Videos are informative and attractive.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1. On task setup, experimental description, and missing information. Even as a reviewer familiar with this domain, I was unable to determine the following key information from the paper alone, prior to inspecting the released codebase. 1. Source of 3D models for clinical cases. How are the 3D vessel models for the 20 multi-center clinical cases obtained? Via the same multi-view angiographic reconstruction pipeline in Sec 2.1? Or from CTA? If from angiographic reconstruction, how many views are used? What reconstruction method is applied? What are the spatial resolution and reconstruction error? 2. Multi-view temporal synchronization. If multi-view angiographic reconstruction is used, clinical views are typically acquired in different cardiac cycles (weak async), meaning vessel morphology differs across views due to cardiac motion. Is ECG-gating used to select images from the same cardiac phase? How is this handled? [8] (AutoCAR) specifically addresses this dynamic sparse-view reconstruction problem. 3. Coordinate dimensionality. Are the input coordinates g_i, c_j in R^2 or R^3? This is never explicitly stated. SOFA is a 3D simulator; rotation actions degenerate under 2D projection; nearest-neighbor matching between guidewire and centerline requires the same dimensionality, all suggesting 3D. But this directly bears on the claim of “from angiographic observations” (2D angiography only provides 2D information). 4. Dynamic modeling and simulation. [5] (Scarponi, IROS 2024) explicitly models cardiac-motion-induced vessel wall deformation as a core contribution. What level of dynamic modeling does CAG-WM provide in comparison? If cardiac motion is not modeled, what exactly is the “real” data experiment? Is it direct XA observation, or a static rendering? THESE INFORMATION MATTERS BECAUSE they prevent reader from assessing several key claims made in the paper, including “the first,” “real world/data,” and the purported differences from [3,4,5]. More specially, some related works I list below(I am not asking author to compare these methods bacuase they may not release thier code or data, but the thing is you should at least EITHER clarify the difference compared with them, in terms of method, task setup, eval way; OR report what is conducted in the exp and method in a clear and more descriptive language). In fact there are many and I can’t list them all, e.g. CathSim. ``` [4] Robertshaw, MICCAI 2025 Anatomy: Aortic arch → carotid/cerebral (MT) Core algorithm: TD-MPC2 Simulator: SOFA Vessel model: 10 real patient CTA Observation input: Guidewire tip coords (3D) Dynamic vessel: No Test environment: SOFA simulation Open-source code: No Comments: Same backbone as CAG-WM; 65% SR on aortic arch [5] Scarponi, IROS 2024 Anatomy: Coronary Core algorithm: SAC Simulator: SOFA Vessel model: Real CTA Observation input: Guidewire tip coords (3D) Dynamic vessel: Yes (cardiac motion) Test environment: SOFA simulation Open-source code: No Comments: Directly comparable anatomy; explicit cardiac dynamics [6] Schegg, RoboSoft 2022 Anatomy: Coronary Core algorithm: Planning-based (MPC) Simulator: SOFA Vessel model: Real CTA Observation input: Guidewire + vessel geometry Dynamic vessel: No Test environment: SOFA simulation Open-source code: No Comments: Directly comparable anatomy; planning approach CAG-WM (this paper) Anatomy: Coronary Core algorithm: TD-MPC2 + TCN encoder Simulator: SOFA Vessel model: 100 synthetic (EG3D) + 20 clinical (source ?) + 10 VMR Observation input: Guidewire coords + centerline coords + target (2D or 3D ?) Dynamic vessel: “Diffeomorphic displacement field” (source and physical meaning ?) Test environment: SOFA simulation (described as “real clinical cases”) Open-source code: Yes Comments: SR 84.7% — but is the difference due to anatomy, encoder,reward, or data volume? No discussion provided. ``` 2. On overclaiming. Below I identify several instances where the paper’s claims appear to exceed what the experiments actually demonstrate. Due to the missing details above, some of these assessments are based on my inference rather than certainty. “End-to-end from angiographic observations” vs. what appears to be an image to point extraction to RL agent pipeline. Evidence from the paper: The Abstract states the method “learns…from angiographic observations in an end-to-end manner.” The Introduction criticizes [4] for “lack[ing] an end-to-end mapping from angiographic images to navigation actions,” implying CAG-WM achieves this. Section 2.3 writes: “given a synthesized angiography image I_t, we detect the stenosis target p*, track the guidewire to obtain N points {g_i} [12], and extract vessel centerline C [26].” Yet the same paper states: “All perceptual information required by observation is pre-extracted prior to training.” Analysis by training/testing phase: During training , all information is directly available from the SOFA simulator, guidewire node positions {g_i} are internal simulator state (no detection network [12] needed); centerlines {c_j} are pre-extracted from the 3D model in Sec 2.1; target p* is manually specified on the centerline. The paper acknowledges this. During testing , clinical vessel geometries are imported into SOFA (see below), so testing also occurs within the simulator. Guidewire coordinates, centerlines, and targets can therefore be directly read from the simulator at test time as well. On the citation of [12] and [26]: The references to a guidewire detection CNN [12] and a centerline extraction method [26] in Sec 2.3 create the impression that these features are extracted from angiographic images. However, within a simulation environment, this information is directly accessible from the simulator and these vision algorithms would not need to be (and likely are not) executed. These citations appear to gesture at a future deployment pipeline rather than describe the current system’s actual data flow. I ask the authors to clarify explicitly: are [12] and [26] actually run during training or testing? Is the image encoder jointly trained? Does the angiographic image enter the network at all? Perception error propagation: If the method were truly deployed clinically on live angiographic images, it would require a complete perception front-end (guidewire detection + centerline extraction + target localization), and errors in each module would propagate to navigation performance. This gap is not discussed. I suggest the authors discuss this at least qualitatively, even without new experiments. Dependency: The missing coordinate dimensionality from W1 exacerbates this issue, if inputs are confirmed to be 3D, the contradiction with “from 2D angiographic observations” becomes even sharper. “Real clinical cases.” Independent evidence: Fig 3.A displays navigation results for clinical cases, showing both a CAG modality row and a SOFA modality row for each case. This directly confirms that testing is performed within the SOFA simulator, the guidewire is virtual, physical interactions are simulated, and observations are obtained from the simulator. Regardless of how the 3D vessel model is obtained, the operating environment itself is not “real.” A more accurate description would be: “evaluated on simulated environments constructed from 20 clinical coronary geometries,” rather than “evaluated on 20 multi-center clinical cases.” <space is limited, I can not write them all>

title: EdgeCVS: Democratization of surgical AI with a Distilled Edge-Deployable Critical View of Safety (CVS) model
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The clinical motivation is clear 2.The paper is well written and easy to understand.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.For such an application focused paper on tiny ML, the authors should compare with all the relevant state-of-the-art. Since, the primary problem of CVS is segmentation, comparing the performance with the Neural Cellular Automata (NCA) that typically has only thousands of paprameters, is a must. A bit of search in Scholar revealed this paper where a foundation model is distilled into the NCA: https://link. springer. com/article/10.1007/s11548-025-03425-x 2.Figure 2 and 3 contains too much information that is not very easy to comprehend. Consider re-designing those.
reviewer_1_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem. Real-time CPU deployment is very relevant for surgical AI. The experiments are structured around clear ablations. In particular, Figure 4 shows the effect of the proposed components on models of different sizes, and Table 1 shows that the final 5M model remains competitive while being far more efficient in terms of inference speed. Concretely, for the proposed 5M model, performance increases from 58.8 to 63.7 with segmentation supervision, then to 65.2 with distillation, and finally to 68.9 with additional pseudo-labeled data in mAP (teacher at 71.4).
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The methodological novelty is more limited than the paper presentation sometimes suggests. The final gain comes from combining known ingredients: segmentation-based auxiliary supervision, teacher-student learning, and pseudo-labeling. Among these, the gain from distillation itself seems modest (1.5%) compared with the gains from segmentation supervision and adding more pseudo-labeled data. I also found the framing of RQ1 weaker than RQ2 and RQ3.The question of whether the CVS task has lower variability seems partly expected from the fact that the task is already restricted to a specific surgical phase and anatomical region. In addition, the “manifold” analysis is done in the embedding space of a specific pretrained encoder, so this is not an intrinsic property of the raw data itself, but a property of that chosen representation.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: A particularly strong aspect is the claim that CVS assessment lies on a compact, low-diversity visual manifold because it is restricted to a specific surgical phase and anatomy. This is interesting because it gives a principled reason why aggressive compression should work here, rather than treating model shrinking as just an engineering trick. The paper makes especially good use of unlabeled videos by restricting pseudo-label generation to the Calot’s triangle dissection phase, where the signal is most relevant. This is a strong data-centric idea: instead of adding arbitrary more data, the method adds task-aligned data density, which is more meaningful for a compact model. Compressing from a 305M-parameter teacher to a 5M-parameter student while staying close to SOTA performance is a major strength. The paper does not just show a smaller model works; it shows that a model with about 1.5% of the teacher’s size can still recover much of the teacher’s decision quality. The deployment story is unusually strong. The paper reports real-time CPU inference above 40 FPS, which directly supports the claim that the method could run on ordinary hospital hardware rather than requiring specialized GPUs. The method is compared against recent CVS challenge teams and prior Endoscapes baselines, and remains competitive despite using vastly fewer parameters. This strengthens the claim that the contribution is not just efficiency in isolation, but an efficiency–accuracy frontier improvement.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The paper’s strongest practical result is real-time CPU inference, which is important. But there is no prospective study, no user study with surgeons, no analysis of whether the system changes decisions in the OR, and no evidence that it improves safety outcomes. So, the “democratization of surgical AI” claim is only partially demonstrated. A big part of the gain comes from densifying the training manifold using teacher-generated classification and segmentation pseudo-labels. However, the paper does not provide much calibration, confidence filtering, or error analysis of those pseudo-labels. That matters because a compact student can also inherit systematic teacher mistakes.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. We address the major concerns below. Task definition (R1): R1 states “the primary problem of CVS is segmentation” and suggests missing benchmarking against tiny ML segmentation models. We respectfully clarify: the benchmarked task is CVS multi-label classification - predicting whether each Critical View of Safety (CVS) criterion is met, evaluated on SAGES-CVS and Endoscapes benchmarks, which define our SOTA scope. Segmentation is used exclusively as an auxiliary training signal; the segmentation head is discarded at inference and no segmentation metrics are reported. The NCA method (eNCApsulate) suggested by R1, addresses segmentation and depth estimation on capsule endoscopy - a different task, anatomy, modality, and benchmark - with no published results on any CVS dataset, making the comparison infeasible. Missing tiny ML SOTA comparison (R1): EdgeCVS is not a tinyML models benchmarking study, it is a data-centric, dual-modality distillation framework that exploits task-specific manifold structure to enable extreme compression. The framework is backbone-agnostic; EdgeNeXT-Small was selected as a strong representative within the established 2.5-10M parameter edge deployment range. The correct evaluation is therefore vertical: how close does the student get to the teacher and SOTA on CVS benchmarks (Table 1 & Figure 4). To the best of our knowledge, no lightweight method has published results on SAGES-CVS or Endoscapes. Manifold analysis (R3): We acknowledge that measuring dispersion in a pretrained embedding space is representation-dependent and falls short of intrinsic dimensionality (ID) metrics. However, classical ID analysis is not directly applicable to video data, as estimates are dominated by temporal autocorrelation between neighboring frames, violating the i.i.d. assumption these metrics require. Using the EVA02-Large embedding space, the source of the distillation signal itself, was our most principled available proxy. We will acknowledge this representation dependency as a limitation in the final manuscript. Methodological novelty (R3): While individual components are established, their contribution lies in unification: MTL, KD, and phase-gated semi-SL are not independent modules but three expressions of a single data-centric dual-modality distillation process, coupling soft classification and segmentation predictions across seen and unseen phase-gated data to probe edge model compression limits. This unification produces a non-trivial result: in general vision tasks, compressing a large model to a small one keeps a significant gap, EdgeCVS substantially closes it on the CVS task. The modest +KD gain in isolation is precisely what reveals this: the bottleneck is not signal quality on existing annotated data but manifold coverage on unseen data, distinguishing EdgeCVS from standard distillation. The contribution is both a deployable surgical AI solution and a transferable hypothesis: task-specific manifold structure determines compression potential, a principle we demonstrate on CVS and propose for similar phase-gated tasks. Pseudo-label quality (R4): To mitigate teacher noise, pseudo-label generation averaged logits across multiple training epochs to reduce variance. Both classification and segmentation pseudo-labels were generated as soft labels encoding the teacher’s probabilities, propagating the teacher’s uncertainty rather than noisy hard pseudo-labels. The consistent gains from +MTL and +SemiSL across all four model sizes in Figures 3 & 4 suggest soft pseudo-labels encode reliable signals. We will update the manuscript accordingly. Prospective clinical validation (R4): The current work establishes the technical foundation, a deployable model retaining large teacher performance, that we hope will enable and inspire such clinical studies. We will revise the manuscript to frame clinical validation as future work enabled by this contribution.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper studies the feasibility of a real‑time CPU‑based surgical AI for automated CVS assessment, with a clear clinical motivation and a strong emphasis on deployability. Reviewers acknowledge that demonstrating a 5M‑parameter model that remains competitive while being far more efficient, achieving real‑time CPU inference, is practically relevant. However, there is consensus that the methodological novelty is limited, as the approach largely combines known components; segmentation‑based supervision, teacher–student learning, and pseudo‑labeling, and that the gain from distillation itself appears modest relative to other components. For an application‑focused paper on tiny ML, a key concern is the missing comparison with relevant lightweight state‑of‑the‑art models, which weakens the positioning of the contribution. Additional concerns include that the manifold analysis is representation‑dependent, that analysis of pseudo‑label quality is limited, and that claims regarding broader impact are only partially demonstrated. Authors should address each concern raised by the reviewers, clarify their positioning, justify methodological choices, and appropriately contextualize claims. | The rebuttal convincingly addresses one major concern by clarifying that the task is classification (not segmentation), making some suggested comparisons less relevant. However, other key issues remain: limited novelty (combining known components like distillation, segmentation supervision, and pseudo-labeling), lack of comparison to lightweight baselines, and limited analysis of pseudo-label quality and broader impact. These points cannot be fully resolved by clarification alone. Despite this, the reviewers lean towards Acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): While there is clear motivation for the work, the paper still lacks technical novelty and clinical validation. The rebuttal addresses some of the raised concerns but not adequately to clear the major issues. Therefore, I recommend a rejection. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After reading the paper and reviews post-rebuttal my opinion is for the paper to be accepted. I believe the work deals with an important and open problem of (edge deployment) with a method that presents interesting novelty. The validation is comprehensive.

title: Robotic Ultrasound Makes CBCT Alive
reviewer_1_strengths: The introduction of the USCorUNet to continuously estimate deformation fields from US streams is technically sound. It elegantly bridges the gap between the high refresh rate of US and the static nature of CBCT. The integration of calibrated alignment with deep learning-based deformation estimation demonstrates a comprehensive understanding of robotic ultrasound-guided surgical systems. The achieved real-time performance is crucial for intraoperative deployment.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Ultrasound imaging is notoriously susceptible to artifacts such as acoustic shadowing, speckle noise, and signal dropouts. The paper lacks a detailed discussion or specific experiments on how USCorUNet handles sudden drops in US image quality. The description of the validation dataset in the current manuscript could be more detailed. It is not entirely clear to what extent the framework was validated on highly realistic in-vivo data versus idealized phantoms. Phantom studies, while valuable for baseline metrics, often fail to replicate the complex non-rigid deformations and heterogeneous textures of real human tissue.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The authors provide a full pipeline from hand-eye calibration, LC2-based rigid refinement, deformation estimation, to CBCT slice updating. This is a valuable engineering contribution for robotic ultrasound-guided interventions. 2.Since ground-truth deformation fields are unavailable for ultrasound, the method distills pseudo-labels from RAFT optical flow, then refines them with confidence-weighted photometric loss and Jacobian-based folding regularization. This semi-supervised + self-supervised approach is sensible and well-motivated. 3.USCorUNet runs at ~11ms end-to-end, enabling real-time intraoperative use. The local correlation volume and 1/8-resolution decoding strike a reasonable trade-off between accuracy and speed.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The authors state that LC2 searches “within a constrained range” after calibration initialization, but no numerical values (e.g., translation/rotation limits) or validation of convergence range are provided. 2.Although a Gaussian correction profile is introduced for probe compression, the paper does not quantify the relationship between applied force and deformation estimation error. The model assumes a symmetric convex profile, which may not hold for heterogeneous tissues or off-center indentation. 3.All metrics are indirect (photometric consistency, forward-backward error, folding ratio, bone mask Dice). No validation against physical markers, finite-element simulations, or ex vivo tracked targets is provided. The clinical plausibility of the estimated deformation fields still remains partially unverified. 4.If I understand correctly, the method updates only the single CBCT slice coplanar with the ultrasound plane, not the full 3D volume. This restricts applicability for true 3D navigation.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The manuscript has several strengths. It presents a complete workflow rather than an isolated methodological component, which enhances the translational value of the work and makes the proposed approach more compelling from an application perspective. The idea of leveraging a RAFT-inspired optical flow strategy to capture deformations between consecutive ultrasound frames is interesting and well aligned with the dynamic nature of deformation induced in ultrasound imaging. The validation is also supported by a relatively diverse dataset, including phantom data, and the comparison against other U-Net-based approaches is appreciated. These elements together make the study relevant and potentially impactful.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The methodological contribution would benefit from clearer positioning. Several of the key building blocks of the framework appear related to existing work, including LC2-based multimodal registration, deformable registration approaches, and CBCT updating strategies. My understanding is that the contribution is focused on USCorUNet. As currently presented, the statement of contributions is somewhat misleading. A clearer articulation of what is fundamentally novel in the proposed framework would help the reader better understand the scope. The central problem appears to be the ultrasound-to-ultrasound deformation estimation. However, it is not yet clear how the proposed solution compares with more classical frame-to-frame ultrasound registration strategies, such as a simple NCC-based approaches. This comparison seems particularly important, as it would help establish rationale to whether the proposed method provides a meaningful advantage over simpler and more established alternatives. Another point that would benefit from clarification is how out-of-plane deformation is handled. In addition, the video examples appear to show some discrepancy in the out-of-field ultrasound deformation. It would therefore be helpful for the manuscript to discuss how such deformations are modeled, and more generally, how robust the method is when out-of-plane or out-of-field motion occurs. There are also some concerns regarding the experimental setup and evaluation. The study mentions scans of in vivo forearm and upper-arm ultrasound (Dataset A), but no ethics approval or related statement appears to be provided. The results presented in Table 2 are difficult to interpret without a clear understanding of the force-stratified evaluation protocol. A concise explanation of this protocol would greatly improve the readability and interpretability of the results. The fine-tuning strategy also raises some questions. The manuscript indicates that fine-tuning was performed on different datasets while keeping the train, validation, and test ratios unchanged. As presented, Table 3 seems to report mean results on test sets drawn from datasets that were also used during training or adaptation. This makes it difficult to judge whether the reported improvements reflect true generalization or are partly driven by dataset-specific adaptation. Clarifying this point would be important, particularly for understanding how the method is expected to perform in clinical practice, where the deformation source is not known in advance. Also a discussion of the anticipated robustness and expected performance under such realistic conditions would substantially strengthen the work.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for their careful assessment and summary. We appreciate R1/R2’s encouraging evaluations (recommended Accept) of our full pipeline, USCorUNet design, and accuracy–speed trade-off, R3’s constructive suggestions and recognition of the complete workflow, RAFT-inspired deformation modeling, diverse validation, and translational value, as well as the AC’s summary. Methodology (R3): The reviews highlight our core contributions: (i) a pipeline from hand-eye calibration and LC2 refinement to deformation estimation and CBCT slice updating; (ii) USCorUNet, a lightweight bidirectional network estimating dense deformation without ground-truth labels via RAFT-derived pseudo-labels and semi-/self-supervised losses, running at ~11 ms; (iii) real-time CBCT updating for probe- and externally induced deformations, bridging high-refresh-rate US and static CBCT; and (iv) validation on in vivo and three phantom datasets. As suggested, we will clarify the distinction between established building blocks and our task-specific integration, USCorUNet, and CBCT-updating contributions. Baselines (R3): NCC/block matching (BM) is a useful local patch-tracking reference, but mainly measures local similarity rather than dense, physically plausible deformation. Prior works (Che et al., “Ultrasound Registration …”, Methods 2017; Sotiras et al., “Deformable Medical …”, TMI 2013; Alessandrini et al., “Detailed Evaluation …”, TMI 2016) show that US registration is sensitive to noise/artifacts/decorrelation, and BM can have larger bias/errors than flow-based methods. Thus, we used task-level baselines: RAFT [18] for dense US-US motion, DefCor-Net [9] for force-stratified comparison, and LC2-FFD [4] for CBCT updating. Together with forward-backward (FB) consistency, folding ratio, Dice, and CBCT-update metrics, they assess motion quality, anatomical/physical plausibility, and downstream utility beyond patch similarity. Validation metrics (R1/R2): We use MAE/NCC for alignment, FB residual for inverse consistency, folding ratio for physical plausibility, bone-mask Dice for anatomical marker correctness, and CBCT-update metrics. For shadowing/dropout/speckle decorrelation, the confidence-weighted photometric loss [10] downweights unreliable regions, while Jacobian regularization suppresses implausible folding; Table 1 ablations show worse FB/Dice/folding scores when either confidence or regularization is removed. We agree that FEM/ex vivo tracked targets would further strengthen validation and will state this point; our current evidence combines multi-dataset evaluation with task-level CBCT updating. Scope/out-of-plane motion (R2/R3): The method updates the 2D CBCT slice corresponding to the active 2D US plane; full 3D volume updating is not claimed. Out-of-plane motion is not directly observed by 2D US. Thus, EDT/Gaussian spatial weighting lets deformation decay away from the observed US window, rather than inferring out-of-plane deformation without additional image evidence. Dataset/protocol (R1/R3): Dataset A uses data from DefCor-Net [9], which was collected under IRB approval No. 2022-87-S-KK. Table 2 follows the force-stratified protocol of DefCor-Net: force between robot and probe is synchronized with B-mode frames and grouped into 1–6 N. Table 3 reports regime-level adaptation, not per-test fitting: the probe-adapted model uses only training splits pooled from Datasets B–D, and the external-adapted model only uses the Dataset B training split; all test splits are held out. LC2/Gaussian details (R2): LC2 searches in-plane translations within ±10 CBCT pixels (0.655 mm/pixel) around the projected US position; slice/orientation are fixed by calibrated geometry. The Gaussian profile is a spatial prior for transferring local US motion to the CBCT ROI, not a calibrated force-to-error model. We will clarify this in the camera-ready version. We appreciate all constructive feedback and recognition of our contributions.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper presents a clinically relevant framework for deformation-aware CBCT updating using real-time robotic ultrasound, integrating calibration, registration, deformation estimation, and CBCT slice updating into a complete workflow. title: SAW: Toward a Surgical Action World Model via Controllable and Scalable Video Generation
reviewer_1_strengths: The authors provided a model for the generation of video surpassing all previous efforts. Although the model is built on already available networks their combination is smart. The authors further evaluate the model on downstream experiment demonstrating potential practical utility, which is very important.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Major concerns: My main concern is the use of the term “world model. ” In its standard meaning, a world model predicts future states conditioned on actions, for example in a state-action-next state formulation. In surgical settings, this would typically correspond to predicting future observations based on control inputs or actions sent to the end-effectors. In contrast, SAW appears to be a controllable video generation method guided by prompts, tool-tip trajectories, and tissue affordance, rather than a model of environment dynamics. For this reason, I believe the method is better described as a conditional surgical video generation framework than as a world model. A relevant prior work in this context is Surgical Vision World Model, previously published at MICCAI last year: https://arxiv. org/pdf/2503.02904.That work is more closely aligned with the world model formulation, and I think the distinction should be made clearer here. As written, the current name and framing may be misleading. Please change name and title. Related to the previous point, the statement in the conclusion that this is a “first step toward surgical action world modeling” is difficult to justify. There is already prior work on surgical world models, and this literature is not sufficiently discussed. In particular, the survey “Deep Reinforcement Learning for Surgical Robotics with State and Image Information: A Survey” (https://assets-eu. researchsquare. com/files/rs-8621244/v1_covered_543c3a07-ebe7-4ecc-bbb5-0de157192396.pdf?c=1769506908) describes the current state of the art for surgical world models and related architectures, but it is not cited. I think the paper would benefit from a clearer positioning with respect to these existing works. I also have concerns about the use and interpretation of the evaluation metrics. The paper states that “CD-FVD is sensitive to temporal inconsistencies,” making it relevant for evaluating the temporal consistency of tool-tissue interactions. While this may be true, no reference is provided for this claim, and the paper does not include an analysis showing that CD-FVD indeed reflects tool-tissue interaction quality in this setting. As a result, the relevance of this metric to the specific surgical application remains assumed rather than demonstrated. More generally, the evaluation relies heavily on perceptual metrics such as FVD and CD-FVD, without validating their relationship to surgical realism or tool-tissue interaction fidelity. In my view, this could have been addressed with a relatively small expert evaluation, for example by asking 2–5 surgeons or trained residents to rate short generated clips with respect to tool motion realism, tissue response realism, and plausibility of tool-tissue contact. Such an evaluation would make the conclusions more convincing. Another concern is the claim about the depth consistency loss. The paper states that it introduces a “novel depth consistency loss enforcing geometric plausibility without requiring depth at inference. ” However, the ablation results in Table 2 seem to complicate this interpretation. In particular, the model trained without the depth consistency loss achieves the best FVD and LPIPS values, while CD-FVD is only slightly worse than the full model. This makes the practical benefit of the loss less clear than suggested in the text. I think this part needs a more careful discussion, especially since the current results do not fully support the strength of the claim. Minor: there is a small formatting issue in “12, 044” which should be “12,044” in the abstract.

author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for acknowledging our strengths: Strong performance [R1,R2], with both visual quality & temporal consistency outperforming SOTA models [R2,R3]; novel approach & practical utility [R1]; grounded evaluations across tasks that are highly relevant for surgical AI﹣action recognition & realistic tool-tissue interaction [R1,R2,R3]; and a large-scale dataset (12k segmentations) with tool-tip trajectories, tissue affordance masks & instrument labels [R2,R3], and for feedback. World Model (WM) Definition & Clarity on Conditioning Signals [R1]: While the WM term has historically been associated with state-transition predictors in Reinforcement Learning (RL), we adopt the modern definition of Generative WMs (e.g., [Sora, Genie, SurgVisionWM]). In this context, SAW treats high-dimensional video as the state space and conditions transitions on one or more conditioning (action) signal﹣text prompt, first-frame input, tissue affordance, 2D tool-tip movements, thereby modeling the complex dynamics of the surgical environment. We will clarify this point and cite parallel prior WMs (e.g., SurgVisionWM) in the final version. Depth Consistency (DC) Loss Significance & Clarity [R1,R2,R3]: Paired bootstrap significance test on our ablation results confirms that the DC loss significantly improves CD-FVD (199.19 vs 207.59, p<0.05), a metric more sensitive to temporal inconsistency (Ge et al. cited [5]). This shows the importance of DC loss in our work in achieving realistic tool and tissue movement. Unlike GeoVideo’s global 3D reprojection, SAW applies a local Smooth-L1 term that reconstructs depth from RGB video tokens, improving the realism of tool-tissue movements without requiring depth at inference. We will better describe the DC loss in the revised Fig. 1 (currently 1c). Methodological Novelty [R2,R3]: Our novelty lies in problem formulation and how we extend prior architectures and training strategies to achieve the first highly controllable and scalable surgical action WM. Previous works require dense, expensive signals (segmentation maps, cited [1, 15, 3]). Moreover, we integrate a depth consistency loss that improves tool-tissue interaction quality without requiring depth at inference. Geometric Consistency & Metric Validation [R1,R2]: Because perceptual-level metrics cannot directly assess the accuracy of tool–tissue interactions, we leverage CD-FVD, which is sensitive to temporal inconsistencies (Ge et al. cited [5]). This implicitly evaluates irregular tool-tissue motion. Additionally, our downstream action-recognition model, trained on SAW-generated data, shows improved performance on real test data, highlighting the realism of the generated tool-tissue interactions. Expert rating of SAW-generated videos will be included in our future work. Downstream task results [R2,R3]: Thank you for highlighting this. SAW-generated data only improves 5/8 actions, because we only augment underrepresented actions (cutting & clipping). Among these, 3/4 show drastic improvements (F1), with a marginal decrease in the fourth. There is also no comparable off-the-shelf model to ours in synthesizing highly realistic action videos. We outperform the closest model (SurgSora) across the major metrics of interest. Representation of Tool-Tip Trajectory [R2]: Representing the tool-tip trajectory through the R/G channels was a careful design choice to reformulate a video-to-video diffusion to a world model. This conditioning input can thus be easily extended to synthesize action videos from a simple sketch of the tool path by the user. IC-LoRA clarity [R2]: IC-LoRA is a parameter-efficient finetuning strategy that allows for frame-by-frame control with a conditioning video. We will include its description and cite it (In-Context LoRA for Diffusion Transformers, Huang et al.) Fig 1 clarity [R2]: We will revise the fig to include each module label & training state (frozen vs. trainable).

title: SMART-KNEE: Sparse-Morphology Based Anatomical Reconstruction Using Topology-Aware Networks for Imageless Total Knee Arthroplasty
reviewer_1_strengths: The technical formulation is sophisticated and well tailored to the surgical usecase. Using an E(3)-equivariant graph neural network is a strong design choice, as it ensures the network can accurately predict landmarks regardless of the arbitrary coordinate frame transformations inherent to intraoperative optical tracking. The system demonstrates impressive accuracy, significantly outperforming baselines like VN-EGNN in landmark prediction, and achieving surface reconstruction errors well below the 3 mm threshold generally accepted for clinical viability in TKA. Splitting the pipeline into a sparse structural prediction and dense morphological generatio elegantly constrains the generative model, ensuring anatomical plausibility.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The study predicates its clinical narrative heavily on the assumption that robotic or highly navigated systems (which require 3D models) are the definitive standard of care. However, conventional TKA remains the standard in many regions, making the clinical motivation somewhat unstable. Framing this as a mandatory solution for the “standard” workflow is slightly overstated. While the methodology is great, the validation is restricted to in-silico metrics and a pristine physical phantom. In a real world intraoperative setting, acquiring the anchor points and sparse point clouds is complicated by soft tissue, cartilage thickness, blood, and surgeon variability. It remains unclear how robust the system is to noisy input data derivd from a real patient
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Structured decomposition via anatomy-aware intermediate representation. The primary strength of this work lies in its formulation of imageless reconstruction as a structured two-stage problem, where anatomical landmark completion serves as an explicit intermediate representation between sparse intraoperative observations and dense surface reconstruction. This design is conceptually meaningful and non-trivial, as it introduces a clinically interpretable and geometrically constrained representation that reduces ambiguity in downstream generation. Unlike end-to-end implicit reconstruction approaches, this decomposition leverages anatomical priors in a modular manner, improving both stability and interpretability. 2.Topology-aware E(3)-equivariant modeling for landmark completion. A key methodological novelty is the integration of topology-aware graph modeling with E(3)-equivariant neural networks for anatomical landmark prediction. By explicitly encoding anatomical structure as a graph and enforcing equivariance under rigid transformations, the method ensures geometric consistency across varying poses and sparse inputs. This approach goes beyond conventional regression or statistical shape models by enabling structured propagation of anatomical constraints, which is particularly effective for recovering unobserved or geometrically distant landmarks. 3.Dual-conditioned generative reconstruction with anatomical constraints. The proposed reconstruction framework introduces a dual-conditioning mechanism that integrates local geometric evidence (partial point clouds) with global anatomical structure (predicted landmarks). This design provides a more controlled and anatomically grounded generative process compared to purely data-driven shape completion methods. Additionally, constraining the generator within a pretrained latent geometry manifold enhances realism and stability, representing a meaningful step toward reliable patient-specific reconstruction in clinical environments. 4.High clinical relevance with imageless and low-input requirements. The work demonstrates strong translational potential by achieving clinically acceptable reconstruction accuracy without reliance on preoperative CT or MRI. This significantly reduces the dependency on imaging resources while maintaining geometric fidelity, addressing a critical limitation in current ITKA systems. The ability to operate under minimal intraoperative input, combined with end-to-end validation, highlights the practical value of the approach for real-world surgical navigation scenarios.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Moderate level of methodological novelty with room for clearer differentiation. The methodological novelty of the framework is moderate and could be better articulated. While the integration of a topology-aware EGNN with an anatomy-aware GAN is well-motivated and tailored to the ITKA scenario, the core components themselves are based on established architectures. As such, the contribution is primarily reflected in the system-level design and problem formulation rather than in fundamentally new modeling techniques. To strengthen the novelty claim, the authors could more explicitly highlight what new capabilities emerge from this integration, for example through targeted ablation studies demonstrating the necessity of topology-aware modeling, or by providing theoretical or empirical analysis showing advantages over alternative architectural combinations. 2.Implicit reliance on learned statistical priors. Despite being framed as an imageless reconstruction approach, the method still relies on implicit statistical priors learned from data. The GAN-based reconstruction stage encodes population-level anatomical distributions within its latent space, effectively replacing explicit statistical shape models (SSMs) with learned priors. This raises a conceptual concern regarding whether the method truly overcomes the limitations of SSM-based approaches or simply shifts the dependency to a different representation. The authors could address this by providing experiments that evaluate generalization beyond the training distribution, such as testing on out-of-distribution anatomies or reduced training data settings, and by explicitly comparing the behavior of the model with classical SSM-based methods in terms of adaptability and bias. 3.Idealized assumptions on intraoperative input quality. The method relies on assumptions about the quality and distribution of intraoperative inputs that may be optimistic in practice. It assumes the availability of well-distributed anchor landmarks and relatively structured sparse surface point clouds, whereas real surgical data may be significantly noisier, incomplete, or unevenly distributed due to occlusion and acquisition constraints. This limits confidence in the robustness of the approach under realistic conditions. To improve this aspect, the authors could include robustness experiments by simulating noise, missing landmarks, or partial point clouds, and analyze performance degradation under such conditions to better reflect clinical applicability. 4.Lack of comparison with stronger or more recent baselines. The experimental evaluation lacks comparisons with several strong and relevant baselines from recent literature. In particular, methods based on diffusion models, implicit neural representations (e.g., NeRF, occupancy networks), or modern shape completion frameworks are not considered. Without such comparisons, it is difficult to assess the relative advantage of the proposed approach in the broader context of contemporary 3D reconstruction methods.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: the proposed method may provide a time-effective and robust method for a well-established problem the emphasis on a minimal set of intraoperatively collected landmark points is important The Topology-Aware Equivariant Graph Neural Network and Anatomy Aware GAN combination is novel The experimental validation is sound and thorough

author_feedback: (1)Meta-Review & R2.7.2 Shape-model-based reconstruction methods [1,12] share two structural limitations (i) Reconstruction is confined to a fixed statistical shape space (linear PCA subspace or deformable template), producing mean-biased outputs for typical morphologies (ii) Fitting requires 15–30 sparse landmark correspondences vs. SMART-KNEE’s 4 anchors. The L_patch coverage loss anchors reconstruction to observe intraoperative geometry, making the manifold a regulariser rather than a mean-shape generator absent in these methods. This is consequential as sparser inputs raise susceptibility to mean-biased reconstruction, propagating error into implant sizing and alignment. (iii) SMART-KNEE’s topology-aware conditioning preserves patient-specific fidelity under this sparse regime (mean T-ASD 1.69 mm vs. 3 mm threshold [18]). SSM infer anatomy by fitting a learned statistical shape space to sparse observations, reporting single-bone partial-surface error (Nolte et al. [12]: 2.60–2.95 mm, femur) or mechanical-axis deviation below 3.5°, whereas SMART-KNEE reconstructs complete F/T morphology from four anchors plus local patches (landmark RMSE 0.25/0.36 mm, ASD 2.4/1.7 mm F/T). Table 2 isolates the gain to prove that SMART-KNEE outperforms VN-EGNN [15] and EquiPPIS [14] by 4–6×. (2) Meta-Review, R1 & R2.7.3 Phantom validation and intraoperative noise.We correct a mischaracterisation , the evaluation (Fig. 5) is not in-silico. The phantom is a 3D-printed physical bone model from a real patient’s CT-segmented STL, complemented by 3D-printed models spanning ±2σ of the dataset’s morphological range (small/large condylar geometries, varus/valgus variants). Anchors and surface patches were acquired with a clinical-grade optical tracker and probe under realistic probe-tip noise, operator variability, and coordinate-frame perturbations not idealised input confirming robustness under practical acquisition conditions. Ground truth is CT-derived. Physical phantom evaluation with optical tracking is the established pre-clinical for surgical navigation [5,16,18] quantifying accuracy under clinical conditions prerequisite before cadaveric trials. Sub-millimetre accuracy on physically fabricated, optically tracked models establishes algorithmic validity necessary for translational progression. Anchor sensitivity analysis further quantifies robustness: errors reach 2.28/1.65 mm under suboptimal distributions vs. 0.25/0.36 mm under standard protocol. Systematic noise injection experiments (missing landmarks, partial occlusion) are a planned extension. (3) R2.7.1 & R2.7.4 Novelty and baselines. System-level novelty resides in three jointly necessary design choices Four sparse landmarks as a clinically interpretable anatomical intermediate, topology-aware E(3) equivariant chirality-conditioned completion and dual-conditioning using both global landmarks and intraoperative surface patches. Diffusion-based completion and implicit neural representations (NeRF, occupancy networks) assume 512–2,048 uniformly sampled points SMART-KNEE operates from ~70–100 points in a single surgical window 10–50× sparser. None target sparse landmark-conditioned reconstruction under E(3)-equivariance with anatomical graph constraints adaptation constitutes independent work. (4)R1 Imageless robotic/navigated TKA is a growing workflow [2,3,5,11,16] motivating SMART-KNEE, without implying conventional TKA is obsolete. (5) R3 Minor issues. F (Femur)/T (Tibia) defined at first text use, E(3) defined as equivariance to 3D rotation, translation and reflection “°” to “axis deviation 3.5°” rephrase reference-led sentences Nolte et al. [12] and add metrics over clinically critical resection zones. (6) R1 and R2 Reproducibility. Upon acceptance, we will release the annotated dataset (361 F/T models with landmark annotations), preprocessing pipeline, training code, and pretrained weights for full reproducibility.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The submission received mixed reviews with one reviewer recommending acceptance, based on novelty of the method and significance of dataset, and two reviewers recommending rejection. The authors should address in the rebuttal the issues raised by the reviewers. In particular I would like to hear about the following: There are currently several navigation/robotic systems in the field for TKA that are imageless and leverage SSM, many times constrained by anatomical landmarks, to obtain a 3D model of femur/tibia. As referred by R2 (point 7.2), and similarly to SSM, the disclosed model also relies on learned statistical priors. Thus, what are the effective benefits with respect to SSM that has proven results in the field for many years, and why should the reader believe on these relative benefits given that the paper only provides results in phantom? | The recommendations remain splitted with two reviewers suggesting acceptance (R1,R3) and one reviewer supporting rejection (R2). I am more aligned with this last recommendation because of the following: SSM is a well established approach that is the cornerstone of several navigation and robotics systems in the feld guiding the execution of thousands of TKA procedures every year (e.g. the Navio/CORI robot). In order to accept the work I would expect reasonable evidence that the proposed approach can outperform SSM in a clinically meaningful manner. The generation of such evidence does not necessarily require bioskills in “ex-vivo” specimens and can eventually be accomplished through experiments as the one of Fig 5, but with multiple phantoms that represent the variability of bone shapes, or through simulated acquisiton of landmarks and surface points in a vast annotated database of arthritic knee segmented from CTs or MRI. In my view the important is to compare the proposed approach againts the baseline SSM method in a representative number of bone F and T shapes using a clinical meaningful metric (ASSD, error in bone cut placement, etc). The authors only argue that conceptually SSM only produces “mean-biased outputs for typical morphologies” and provide a single experiment in phantom without any comparison with other methods that only shows that the their method can work in practice. This is clearly insufficient and for this reason my recommendation is to reject the paper Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I am aligning with the two accept decisions. This is a strong CAI paper and should be evaluated within that context. The authors have also clarified and addressed several major misunderstandings raised during the review process. While the current evaluation remains limited to a highly controlled experimental setting, future cadaver and clinical studies will be important next steps to further demonstrate the practical and clinical value of the proposed approach. Nevertheless, the work presents sufficient novelty and technical merit to warrant presentation at the meeting, and I believe it will generate significant interest and discussion within the CAI community. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Reviewers appreciated the comprehensive rebuttal, which resolved concerns about the validation on physical 3D phantoms using optical tracking. There was also a strong argument why NeRF and diffusion are unsuitable for this task, given the sparsity of surgical point clouds. While the authors should reduce the claim of clinical readiness (R2) in light of the current evaluation on physical phantom, this level of evaluation is appropriate for a CAI paper, and the paper should generate interest at the conference.

title: Surgical Anatomy Recognition with Context Learning using Foundation Representations
reviewer_1_strengths: Substantial dataset contribution. ATLAS-120k is the first surgical anatomy segmentation dataset spanning 14 procedures with both laparoscopic and robot-assisted videos, representing a meaningful advance over existing single-procedure datasets. Well-motivated method design. The incorporation of procedure and phase context queries directly targets a genuine domain gap, namely that surgical anatomy segmentation requires procedural awareness beyond pure visual tracking, and the motivation is clearly articulated. Comprehensive evaluation. The comparison covers natural-image, medical, and surgical foundation models with detection, segmentation, and temporal consistency metrics, providing a thorough picture of the state of the art. Real-time feasibility. 64 FPS on an H100 is a practically meaningful result for intraoperative guidance applications.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Annotation quality validation is insufficient. The annotation pipeline relies heavily on automated propagation with manual correction, yet no inter-annotator agreement metric is reported. Surgeon review is described only for the first frame of each clip, leaving the quality of propagated frames unverified beyond the correction step. Given that ATLAS-120k is a primary contribution, a more rigorous quality analysis, including an estimate of propagation error rates and correction frequency, is essential. Class imbalance and exclusion criteria are underreported. Training is restricted to 30 of 42 classes by excluding categories absent from all splits and merging semantically similar ones. The paper does not specify which classes were excluded or merged, nor does it report per-class performance. Ablation contains an inconsistency. In Table 3, adding temporal query propagation to the in-domain pretrained model increases AP (0.57→0.59) but decreases mDice (0.43→0.36) and mVC metrics. This counterintuitive drop in segmentation quality is not discussed. Understanding this trade-off is important for interpreting the overall contribution of temporal propagation.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper presents a very important video anatomy segmentation dataset benchmark that will be beneficial to the entire community. The dataset has much higher quality than previous ones. The idea of using context in video models, such as phase- and procedure-related information, is interesting.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1)The authors claim things that they do not evaluate/demonstrate. For example, they claim to introduce a real-time framework, #INTRODUCTION: “real-time anatomical segmentation”, yet they do not show any time-related metric. 2) The authors do not present any final loss function for their training; instead, they have a block of text in page 7, which is very non-standard, that literally describes the total loss they used. This is very unacceptable. The total loss must’ve been described in the Methods section, and coefficients of the loss function with mathematical symbols, and in the experiment setup, the values of those coefficients must have been outlined using their symbols; this is basic writing etiquette. 3) The main table of results, Tables 2 and 3, all look green and red. In academic papers, usually the use of a color/line is to indicate the best model, and maybe another one to indicate the second-best model, to outline the GAIN compared to the previous best model. Your tables do not look good visually, the color green is everywhere, you have then highlighted in red the worst performing model, I have never seen this in a paper before. 4) The in-domain pretraining was never mentioned in the Methods section, which is considered an important component of the framework, and only in the Experiments section; this is wrong. 5) Clarity and good presentation is important in a paper, I believe Section 2 to not be fully clear. For example, there is no specific pipeline figure to outline the main contribution of the pipeline, which is phase and procedure-specific queries. Fig1.Acts more as showing the difference between current and past approaches. Another example, It is unclear if authors have built upon VidEoMT or EoMT at the end (second paragraph of page 3, as they start talking about EoMT and then switch to VidEoMT in between. 6) In the Experiments section (4), when mentioning the split, the authors do not mention whether they make sure the distribution of procedures remains balanced or similar in the data splits or not, which can highly affect results and interpretations. 7) The authors have chosen to have page 7 with all text, and have the related results on the following page. reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The introduction of ATLAS-120k addresses an important limitation in existing surgical datasets. The dataset is notable for its diversity, with annotations spanning many procedures and anatomical classes, and for its human-in-the-loop annotation pipeline involving expert supervision and verification. By explicitly modeling procedure and phase queries, the design reflects the idea that anatomical visibility and interpretation depend strongly on the context of the current procedure, and benefits surgical segmentations.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.While the experiments show that ATLAS outperforms the compared baselines, the absolute performance remains modest, with the best reported results at AP 0.64 and mDice 0.49.Although authors state that the low mDice score proves the challenge of the dataset, this counters the technical contributions of the proposed method in the class-imbalanced and long-tail distribution setting. The paper does not report results of experiments conducted on other surgical segmentation benchmarks, so it is difficult to determine that ATLAS has extended capabilities in anatomy recognition and scene understanding. 2.The dataset construction and annotation workflow require further clarification. It remains unclear how extensive the human supervision was beyond the first frame and how propagation errors were identified and corrected in practice. Additionally, the object tracking model was iteratively fine-tuned in the annotation process, but the metrics are not reported for the performance of initially annotated frames. Since the tracking model is not designed specifically for the medical domain, errors in the initial propagation could potentially bias later stages unless corrected carefully. Therefore, further explanation of the annotation quality control would be helpful.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers (R1–R3) for their careful feedback. All three recognize ATLAS-120k as a meaningful contribution and appreciate the context-aware design of ATLAS. We have grouped the reviewer feedback into the following sections. Reproducibility and Real-Time Claim [R1 (general), R2 (1)] Two points may not have been clear: (1) R1’s reproducibility concern: the code, models, annotations, and annotation platform will be publicly released upon acceptance (Abstract, final sentence). (2) R2’s real-time concern: ATLAS ViT-L achieves 64 FPS on an H100 GPU (Section 4, page 7), supporting our real-time claim. Annotation Quality and Pipeline Reliability [R1 (1), R3 (2)] The annotation pipeline was human-in-the-loop throughout the entire process, not only at initialization. Propagated annotations for all frames were systematically inspected and corrected by surgical research fellows before being accepted. The tracking model was iteratively refined at 10k, 25k, and 50k frames, each followed by additional correction rounds to mitigate drift and ensure consistency. Statistics on correction frequency were not recorded during dataset construction. However, annotation quality was ensured through a final surgeon review of the first frame, followed by a final inspection of all frames by a research fellow. Class Exclusion and Per-Class Reporting [R1 (2)] Classes appearing in fewer than three videos were excluded because, under the patient-level split (70/10/20 videos), such classes would not reliably appear across all splits, making evaluation unstable or infeasible. Fine-grained subclasses with insufficient coverage were merged into parent categories (e.g., specific arteries → “artery”, specific ducts → “duct”). Per-class results are available but omitted due to space constraints; they will be released on GitHub upon acceptance. Ablation Inconsistency: Temporal Propagation and mDice [R1 (3)] R1 rightly flags this as counterintuitive. While we cannot draw hard conclusions, this may be explained by how the metrics differ. AP rewards consistent instance detection, so a propagated query that reliably localizes an instance can improve AP even with imprecise boundaries. mDice, however, is a pixel-level metric aggregated over the full frame, making it more sensitive to boundary drift in propagated frames. The full ATLAS model recovers and surpasses all metrics (AP: 0.64, mDice: 0.49), suggesting context queries counteract this effect. We will clarify this in the final version. Presentation and clarification [R2 (2-8)] We acknowledge these presentation issues, which require only minor textual and structural revisions. We will move in-domain pretraining and the training loss to the Methods section, formalize the loss as an equation, clarify procedure balance across splits, improve the EoMT→VidEoMT→ATLAS description, and balance tables and text. Figure 1 will be revised into a clearer pipeline diagram. The DINO ablation results will be retained as they show meaningful differences in mDice and mVC. On table formatting: color gradients were used to convey nuanced relative performance; we will consider revising toward standard best/second-best highlighting. Generalization and Benchmark Scope [R3 (1)] Our primary contribution is demonstrating consistent improvements over strong baselines in the challenging multi-procedure setting of ATLAS-120k, the only available dataset of this scope. We did not specifically target long-tail class imbalance and did not intend to imply this. We do hypothesize that context queries may help identify underrepresented classes, as the additional context could guide the model toward anatomy that is rare overall but expected within a specific procedure or phase. However, we did not investigate this explicitly and consider it an interesting direction for future work. We performed a zero-shot evaluation on other datasets, but it was omitted due to page limits and will be considered in future work.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper introduces ATLAS‑120k, a large‑scale surgical anatomy segmentation dataset covering 14 procedures and multiple modalities, along with a video segmentation model that leverages procedure‑ and phase‑aware context queries. Reviewers consistently recognize the dataset as a major and valuable contribution, filling an important gap beyond single‑procedure benchmarks, and agree that incorporating procedural context is well motivated. Nonetheless, key concerns remain regarding limited validation of annotation quality, incomplete reporting of class exclusions and imbalance handling, and an unexplained ablation behaviour where temporal propagation improves AP while degrading segmentation metrics. Further issues relate to methodological clarity and presentation, including incomplete loss specification and claims that are not fully supported by the reported results. Clearer documentation of annotation reliability, improved methodological transparency, and ensuring the claims are fully supported by the evaluation would strengthen the overall contribution. Authors should address each concern raised by the reviewers. Moreover, authors should refine their technical writing to address the concerns about lack of experimental details, non standard notations, and figures. | The rebuttal addresses most key concerns, especially by clarifying the annotation pipeline (human-in-the-loop corrections), explaining class exclusion and imbalance handling, and providing a reasonable explanation for the AP vs mDice inconsistency. It also commits to improving presentation issues (loss definition, figures, writing clarity), which were a major source of concern. Some limitations remain, particularly lack of quantitative annotation quality metrics and incomplete reporting, but these are mitigated by the detailed clarification and the strong dataset contribution. The reviewers agree on Acceptance.
