title: Trajectory-Aware Cross-Paradigm Transformers for Efficient System Matrix Calibration in Magnetic Particle Imaging
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The core innovation of this paper is its explicit physics-informed modeling, this paper cleverly embeds the physical characteristics of SM signal formation into the Transformer architecture. The Trajectory-Aware Encoding Branch (TAEB) explicitly models the relevance between the Field-Free Point (FFP) trajectory and voxels by assigning spatial distance-based importance weights, which provides a strong theoretical foundation and represents a highly novel approach to solving MPI calibration. Furthermore, the proposed Cross-Paradigm Feature Interaction Module (CP-FIM) effectively unites frequency-domain and spatial-domain analyses. Using Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) to process query and key embeddings to capture global channel correlation is an ingenious design that perfectly aligns with the inherent spectral characteristics of MPI signals. 2.The authors utilize the public OpenMPI dataset and conduct rigorous comparative tests across a wide variety of settings. The evaluation spans different nanoparticle materials (Synomag-D, Perimag), distinct FFP scanning trajectories (3D Lissajous, 2D Lissajous), and various upsampling ratios (2x, 4x), firmly validating the generalizability and robustness of the proposed framework.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The current experimental evaluation relies entirely on phantom reconstructions and dataset-based quantitative metrics. While these experiments demonstrate the fundamental efficacy of the method, the absence of in vivo data or downstream clinical tasks makes it difficult to assess the model’s robustness against complex, real-world noise distributions and artifacts. This significantly limits the demonstration of the method’s actual clinical impact and translational potential. 2.Although the authors compare their method against several deep learning baselines (e. g. , SMRnet and TranSMS), the overall selection of baselines remains limited. Apart from these methods, the remaining comparisons are primarily with traditional techniques (e. g. , bicubic interpolation) or methods proposed several years ago. Such a setup does not adequately reflect the current state of the art. To provide a more convincing evaluation, it is recommended to include more recent and advanced approaches—both those specifically developed for MPI system matrix super-resolution and those from the broader natural image super-resolution field (e. g. , recent generative or diffusion-based models). This would allow for a more comprehensive and up-to-date assessment of the proposed method’s performance. 3.Marginal quantitative improvements relative to architectural complexity: While the proposed TACPT-Net achieves the best overall scores, the absolute quantitative gains over the best-performing baselines (e. g. , 3dISPAnet) are somewhat limited. For instance, the improvement in SSIM is roughly 1–2%, and the NRMSE reduction is about 10%. The authors should provide further discussion or visual evidence to justify whether these incremental metric gains translate to clinically meaningful differences in visual fidelity or diagnostic accuracy, justifying the added complexity of the cross-paradigm modules.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: This paper presents a novel Trajectory-Aware Cross-Paradigm Transformer (TACPT) to address the critical bottleneck of time-consuming System Matrix (SM) calibration in Magnetic Particle Imaging (MPI). The primary strength lies in the Trajectory-Aware Encoding Branch (TAEB), which effectively integrates physical priors by embedding voxel-wise distances to the Field-Free Point (FFP) trajectory into the transformer backbone, guiding the model toward information-dense regions. Furthermore, the introduction of a Cross-Paradigm Feature Interaction Module (CP-FIM)—combining FFT-based inter-channel modeling with spatial structural learning—coupled with a Dynamic Sparsity-Gated Fusion Block (DSGFB), allows for the adaptive suppression of redundant noise while preserving compact SM representations. The methodology is rigorously validated on the OpenMPI dataset across diverse nanoparticle materials and scanning trajectories, demonstrating superior reconstruction fidelity with an average relative nRMSE reduction of over 10% compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Despite its technical merits, the paper exhibits certain weaknesses, primarily regarding the lack of computational complexity analysis and a limited discussion on clinical translation. While the model maintains a relatively small parameter count, the integration of Fast Fourier Transforms (FFT) within the CP-FIM and the iterative nature of the sparsemax-based gating in DSGFB may introduce significant inference latency compared to simpler CNN-based baselines like SRCNN. Furthermore, the evaluation relies heavily on standard metrics (nRMSE, PSNR, SSIM) without assessing reconstruction robustness against real-world hardware artifacts or patient motion, which are critical for demonstrating the proposed method’s actual clinical feasibility. Lastly, while the trajectory-aware encoding is a strong addition, the paper would benefit from a more rigorous comparison against emerging implicit neural representation (INR) techniques that have recently shown promise in similar medical imaging super-resolution tasks.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The idea of incorporating trajectory-aware physical priors directly into a transformer architecture for system matrix calibration is interesting, novel and well-motivated. In particular, encoding voxel relevance based on the FFP trajectory and combining it with joint spectral-spatial modeling provides a more physically grounded alternative to existing purely data-driven super-resolution approaches. The framing of the prior is elegant and it proves useful downstream. The paper is also easy to follow, generally well-framed, and key choices made by the authors are well-motivated.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The claim of novelty in incorporating physical knowledge into SM calibration is overstated. TranSMS already integrates physics into the learning process via a data-consistency module that enforces adherence to the forward MPI signal model between low and high-resolution system matrices. In comparison, the current paper introduces a different form of physical integration (trajectory-aware priors), but the general idea of using a physics prior in SM calibration is not new, and this paper should be positioned as an extension of that idea rather than a fundamentally new direction. The baseline comparison is incomplete for a strong SOTA claim. While the paper includes several relevant methods, it omits more recent and closely related MPI calibration approaches that explicitly leverage structural or physical priors, such as ProTSM for structured SM learning (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37471193/), MKD-SM (https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11267072) which exploits inter-slice correlations and prior knowledge , and recent position-prior-guided SM super-resolution methods that directly incorporate positional priors into the model (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.05795). This weakens the positioning of the paper and makes it unclear whether the reported gains would hold against the strongest prior-/knowledge-driven approaches. Some claims are not fully supported by the experiments. In particular, the paper emphasizes improved efficiency and reduced recalibration overhead, but does not provide runtime, acquisition-time, or computational cost analysis, and the trajectory-aware prior itself is based on a heuristic formulation without comparison to alternative physically motivated priors.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers for thorough and constructive comments. Below are point-by-point responses to key concerns. 1.Quantitative Gains, Model Necessity, Efficiency and OOM Risk(R1/R2/R4) The 1-2% SSIM gain over 3dISPAnet is meaningful. Our method consistently outperforms all baselines across six settings, with 6-17% NRMSE reduction vs. LapSRN, 0.3-0.6 dB PSNR gain vs. 3dISPAnet, and 4-20% SSIM improvement vs. traditional interpolation. Small SM errors propagate severely in trajectory-sensitive MPI regions, so stable multi-metric gains matter clinically. Ablations confirm module necessity: TACPT-Net cuts NRMSE from 0.0318 to 0.0202, raises PSNR to 34.60 dB and SSIM to 0.941, with only 0.92M to 1.21M parameters. TAEB and CP-FIM provide complementary, non-redundant gains. In terms of efficiency, TACPT-Net outperforms 3dISPAnet with fewer parameters (1.21M vs. 1.48M), lower FLOPs (1.25G vs. 1.55G), and faster inference (0.11s vs. 0.14s). The sparsemax gating in DSGFB adds negligible overhead, as it is a single sparse operation rather than iterative refinement. The potential OOM issue from dense voxel-trajectory broadcasting is an implementation concern, not a fundamental limitation: relevance maps can be cached; chunk-wise computation supports large FOVs. 2.In Vivo Validation(R1) We agree that in vivo validation will enhance its clinical relevance, and we will mark it as an important future research direction. Currently, publicly available in vivo MPI datasets with paired LR and HR SMs are scarce. We performed validation using real-world open MRI phantom data that incorporates genuine system responses and measurement noise. Phantom validation is a standard practice in recent studies on MRI scan phantom calibration, including TranSMS, 3dISPAnet, and MKD-SM. Our experimental setup follows mainstream practices and enables us to assess the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method. 3.Novelty, Baseline Selection and INR(R2, R4) We explicitly clarify the novelty of our work: our contribution is not the general idea of applying physics priors in SM calibration, but the novel design of trajectory-dependent prior and its representation-level integration into deep networks, including the fourth-order TAEB aware encoding, joint frequency-spatial CP‑FIM, and sparse DSGFB gated fusion. This framework provides a valuable complementary improvement to existing physics-guided calibration methods such as TranSMS. We acknowledge the relevance of the suggested baselines: ProTSM, MKD‑SM, and PPGnet. MKD‑SM and PPGnet were published in late 2025, with no public code or pretrained models available at submission time. Although ProTSM was published earlier, it depends on specialized hyperparameter modeling and a separate pre-training–fine-tuning pipeline. Therefore, fair and verifiable quantitative comparisons cannot be completed in a limited time. To ensure fair and reproducibility, we compared with representative reproducible CNN- and Transformer-based baselines under the same setting, including 3dISPAnet, SMRnet, and TranSMS. In the revised edition, we will discuss these latest methods and include full citations. INR is promising, but direct MPI SM SR is non-trivial because SMs are high-dimensional, multi-channel, and trajectory-dependent; We will add a dedicated discussion about INR and list both INR-based SM modeling and the latest 2025 methods as important future benchmarks. 4.Equation and Code Consistency(R1) All reported results used the fourth-order trajectory distance weighting in Eq. (1). The uploaded TrajB.py was an earlier internal exploratory version, an inadvertent code-release error. We have corrected the code in the anonymous repository, re-ran key checks and confirmed consistency with the reported results. 5.Other Minor Revisions(R1, R4) We will add \titlerunning to fix LaTeX warnings, define “reduced recalibration overhead” clearly, and include full complexity analysis to strengthen efficiency claims.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): Please provide justifications and clarifications for the concerns raised by the reviewers. | This paper proposes TACPT-Net, a physics-informed transformer for MPI system matrix calibration that embeds FFP trajectory priors via a trajectory-aware encoding branch and combines spectral and spatial feature modeling. The core idea of trajectory-aware positional encoding is well-motivated and the ablation study supports the contribution of each component. However, as R1 summarizes concisely in their post-rebuttal assessment, the novelty claims are insufficiently differentiated from existing physics-informed methods given the missing comparison against recent baselines, the experimental validation relies on phantom data with relatively outdated baselines, and key concerns are deferred to future work rather than addressed in the current submission. The rebuttal does not provide concrete justification for why the proposed approach should be superior to these missing methods, which leaves the novelty question open. Thus, this paper is not recommended for acceptance in its current form. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes TACPT-Net, a trajectory-aware cross-paradigm Transformer framework for efficient system matrix calibration in Magnetic Particle Imaging. The method aims to improve sparse SM calibration by incorporating Field-Free Point trajectory priors into the Transformer backbone and jointly modeling frequency-domain and spatial-domain dependencies through cross-paradigm feature interaction. The reviewers recognized the importance of the MPI calibration problem, the novelty of trajectory-aware physical prior integration, and the generally strong performance across different nanoparticle materials, scanning trajectories, and upsampling ratios. In particular, the idea of using FFP trajectory-dependent positional encoding provides a physically grounded alternative to purely data-driven SM super-resolution methods. The reviewers raised concerns about incomplete baseline comparisons, limited validation on phantom data, marginal gains over the strongest baselines, and the lack of computational analysis in the original submission. A more serious concern was the reported mismatch between Eq. (1) and the uploaded code for the Trajectory-Aware Encoding Branch. The authors clarified in the rebuttal that the reported results used the fourth-order trajectory distance weighting described in the manuscript, while the uploaded code was an earlier internal exploratory version, and that the code has since been corrected. They also clarified the novelty as trajectory-dependent representation-level physics integration, provided complexity numbers showing fewer parameters, lower FLOPs, and faster inference than 3dISPAnet, and explained the difficulty of fairly comparing with very recent prior-guided SM calibration methods without public code or pretrained models. Although some limitations remain, especially the lack of in vivo validation and missing quantitative comparisons with the newest prior-/position-guided SM calibration methods, these issues mainly affect the strength of the SOTA and clinical-translation claims rather than invalidating the core contribution. The final version should clearly correct the code/manuscript inconsistency, sharpen the positioning relative to recent physics- and prior-guided MPI calibration methods, and avoid overclaiming clinical impact beyond phantom validation. Overall, the proposed trajectory-aware physics-informed Transformer is technically sound, reasonably novel, and practically relevant for MPI SM calibration. Therefore, I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After rebuttal, I recommend Accept. The paper presents a sound and well-motivated trajectory-aware, physics-informed transformer for efficient MPI system matrix calibration. The rebuttal clarifies that the novelty and it addresses complexity concerns with parameter, FLOP, and inference-time comparisons showing better efficiency than 3dISPAnet. While comparisons to very recent prior-/position-guided methods and in vivo validation would strengthen the work, the authors provide reasonable justification for the current scope. The code-manuscript inconsistency was a concern, but the authors stated that the correct formulation was used for reported results and that the repository has been corrected. Overall, the remaining issues are addressable in revision.

title: VigilSAM3: Reinforcement-Optimized Memory Gating for Ultra-Long Surgical Video Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: Technical Innovation: Using reinforcement learning (GRPO) to solve the sequential decision-making problem of “when to update memory” is a principled and effective approach to mitigating temporal drift. Clinical Relevance: The focus on small, transient structures like “Blood Points” (<0.1% of frame area) is highly relevant to surgical safety. Dataset Contribution: Hepa-Vein appears to be a high-quality, expertly annotated dataset that fills a gap in hepatectomy benchmarks. Strong Empirical Results: The model achieves state-of-the-art performance on both Hepa-Vein and DSAD datasets, particularly showing significant gains in challenging small-target classes.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Fairness of Baselines (Model Versioning): The proposed method is built upon SAM3, while many compared SOTA methods (e. g. , ReSurgSAM2, MedSAM2) are based on the older SAM2 architecture. It is unclear how much of the performance gain is attributed to the SAM3 backbone vs. the proposed RL-scheduling and Memory Firewall. Question: Can the authors provide results where the baseline models (like ReSurgSAM2) are implemented using the same SAM3 backbone for a fairer comparison? Baseline Performance Discrepancy: In Table 1, the performance of MedSAM3 on “Blood Point” (39.32 Dice) is significantly lower than the proposed method (66.73 Dice). Question: Was MedSAM3 specifically fine-tuned for small-target detection on this dataset? Such a large gap suggests the baseline might not have been fully optimized. Real-time Latency Peaks: While the average FPS (22.53) is reported , the system involves a heavy “System 2” detector for corrections. Question: What is the peak latency when the “Correct” or “Reset” actions are triggered? For real-time surgical guidance, the consistency of the frame rate is as important as the average speed. There are minor typographical errors in some table labels (e. g. , “Glison” instead of “Glisson”)
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The motivation of the paper is clear. It shows a strong attempt to solve the limitations of current video segmentation methods when applied to ultra-long videos, especially in the surgical context. The paper is somewhat easy to follow, with good overall structure and organization. All components of the method seem to complement each other and appear necessary, with clear and justified explanations for their inclusion.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Major: Overall lack of related work on long-term surgical segmentation methods. Also, no mention of other works that address memory drift and memory management in video segmentation. Major: The evaluation is selective: the paper reports class-wise scores but omits an overall (full-image) metric. Furthermore, on the DSAD dataset, only 2 out of 8 classes are reported, raising concerns about fairness of the comparison. Comparison methods were also not optimised for rare classes. E.g. nnunet can be trained with class-weighted CE for improved performance on rare classes Needs clarification how video segmentation performance is being evaluated with datasets where annotation is not on complete video The evaluated domain is very limited especially for general segmentation task. Need additional surgical domains (e.g., Cataract-1k, AutoLaparo, ,..) How is temporal continuity handled during the reset action? It would be helpful to also report temporal continuity/smoothness metrics.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Proposed the Hepa-Vein dataset with dense labeling; 2.Good quantitative results were achieved on both the Hepa-Vein and the external DSAD datasets. For the extremely small and intermittently occurring “Blood Point” category, a significant improvement in the Dice score was realized compared to existing methods. 3.By adopting the critic-free GRPO algorithm, the framework avoids the expensive computational overhead associated with approximating value functions in high dimensional long surgical video scenarios
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.This approach introduces excessive computational overhead by deploying expensive RL and detection modules to tackle visibility issues that classical methods solve more efficiently. For instance, kinematic priors provide a more elegant solution for occlusions, and the ByteTrack philosophy demonstrates that low-confidence detections still hold valuable temporal information. A more fundamental flaw lies in the handling of endoscopic camera ego-motion. Without Global Motion Compensation (GMC), treating corrected frames as persistent Anchored Memory creates a spatial mismatch as the lens moves, leading to catastrophic drift rather than stability. 2.The core of the “Hierarchical Memory Firewall” essentially reduces to standard residual fusion and MLP-based gating, offering limited novelty in spatiotemporal modeling. Given that recent medical imaging tasks have shown that Confidence-based Reset mechanisms can effectively mitigate memory drift in occluded scenarios, the complexity of the RL-based approach must be justified. A training-free baseline utilizing simple confidence-triggered resets is mandatory. This would prove that the GRPO agent’s performance stems from genuine causal reasoning over long sequences, rather than simply mimicking a static decision threshold. 3.A critical concern in the proposed architecture is its over-reliance on the perceived authority of System 2.By designating System 2 outputs as persistent anchor, the authors overlook the reality that detectors frequently produce false positives in noisy endoscopic environments. This design creates a positive feedback loop of errors; a single misdetection becomes a permanent reference point, ensuring that the memory remains permanently polluted. Without a verification or aging mechanism for these anchors, the system’s long-term stability is fundamentally compromised.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: Thanks for kind advice. R1 (1) To isolate the SAM3-backbone effect, we built a SAM3-backed ReSurgSAM2-style baseline by preserving credible initialization and diversity-driven memory selection on the official SAM3 detector/tracker. It obtains Dice/IoU 68.14/55.93, while VigilSAM3 obtains 69.18/57.22, suggesting the gain is not merely from SAM3.(2) MedSAM3 releases image-level SAM3 LoRA training but no video memory-propagation recipe. We adapted it with the same first-frame prompt/tracking protocol as our SFT stage, without MF or Correct/Reset. At shorter clip length, MedSAM3 reaches Blood Pt. Dice/IOU of 57.79/46.29.The remaining gap is because pure tracking cannot recover once tiny Blood Points are missed or written inaccurately into memory. In VigilSAM3, Correct/Reset invokes System 2 to generate dense logits S_t conditioned on the existing prompt and draft D_t; S_t refines output and memory. No manual prompt or GT mask is used at inference. (3) On A800, forced Trust/Correct/Reset peaks at 36.3/154.9/143.5 ms. The latter two are sparse, so latency still controllable. (4) We will correct “Glison” to “Glisson”. R2 (1) We will expand related work: STCN/AOT establish memory-based VOS; XMem designs sensory/working/long-term memory; SAM2Long/DAM4SAM address SAM2 error accumulation, distractors, and memory selection; SurgSAM2/ReSurgSAM2 study surgical SAM2 via frame pruning, credible initialization, and diversity-driven memory. We position VigilSAM3 as complementary: it learns Trust/Correct/Reset and gates writes at pixel/class/frame levels. (2) The two DSAD classes originally reported are vascular structures, matching Hepa-Vein’s goal; this was for vascular generalization rather than cherry-picking. We further evaluated 11 DSAD classes: mesenteric artery 74.65, intestinal veins 64.71, abdominal wall 84.21, colon 68.35, pancreas 41.53, spleen 68.99, stomach 82.58, small intestine 65.59, ureter 31.65, vesicular glands 45.74, liver 76.07, with overall Dice/IoU 63.14/52.68, which is competitive with SOTA methods. (3) VigilSAM3 uses no class-weighted segmentation loss; rare-class handling comes from class-aware GRPO reward and per-class memory gating. U-Net/nnU-Net with class-weighted loss obtain Blood Point Dice/IoU 26.05/19.74 and 28.32/21.97.(4) Hepa-Vein is extracted from long raw videos, but all retained benchmark frames are densely annotated; every evaluated frame has a GT mask, with no unlabeled/interpolated/pseudo-labeled frames. (5) For domain breadth, AutoLaparo gives Dice/IoU 87.26/80.91, close to LMS-Net (88/82), supporting generalization beyond hepatectomy and DSAD. (6) For temporal continuity, VigilSAM3 outperforms ReSurgSAM2 on Contour Jitter↓/t-IoU↑: 11.13 vs. 14.47, and 71.65 vs. 65.96; Reset does not introduce discontinuity. R3 (1) The agent is lightweight; main overhead is occasional System-2 invocation, whose latency is bounded. We thank the reviewer for GMC. By adding lightweight GMC variant in the dense-prompt path: for an anchor at frame a, its dense logits are warped to frame t using H_{a->t} before memory conditioning, without changing SAM3 detector/tracker. This improves Dice/IoU from 69.18/57.22 to 69.77/57.69.We will consider this direction for extension. (2) Table 3 isolates SA, MF, and GRPO under the same SAM3 backbone. We added training-free Periodic Correct, Confidence Correct, and Confidence Reset baselines with the same SAM3 detector/tracker and prompt protocol. The best rule baseline is Confidence Reset, but is still 4.48/3.51 lower than VigilSAM3 in Dice/IoU, supporting that GRPO is not mimicking a static threshold and simple non-learning scheduling cannot replace the learned policy. (3) To test false anchors, promoted anchors have mean Dice 92.79 and false-anchor rate 1.63% (Dice<0.3). After anchor promotion, t-IoU is 74.39 and Contour Jitter is 7.08, showing no persistent error feedback loop. We will clarify that Reset removes recent contaminated memory and re-initializes the current state.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The reviewers generally found the paper clinically meaningful and technically promising, and all current recommendations are in the weak-accept range. At the same time, several important concerns were raised that should be addressed carefully in the rebuttal, as they may materially affect the final assessment. First, the rebuttal should clarify the fairness of the experimental comparisons, especially the extent to which the reported gains come from the proposed memory-gating and scheduling design versus the use of a SAM3-based backbone while several competing methods are built on earlier SAM variants. In particular, the comparison to MedSAM3 and other strong baselines would benefit from clearer discussion of whether they were fully optimized under matched settings, especially for the rare and small Blood Point class. Second, the necessity of the RL-based scheduling component should be more convincingly justified. One reviewer explicitly questioned whether simpler non-RL alternatives, such as confidence-threshold-based correction or reset rules, could already recover much of the benefit. A strong rebuttal should therefore clarify whether the gains of the GRPO agent go beyond what can be achieved by straightforward heuristic scheduling, and why the additional complexity is warranted. Third, the evaluation protocol should be clarified and, if possible, strengthened. Concerns were raised regarding selective reporting, including the fact that only two classes are reported on DSAD and that no more global or overall metric is shown. The authors should explain the rationale for this reporting choice, clarify how evaluation is performed when annotations are not available for complete videos, and address whether the conclusions remain consistent under broader reporting. Fourth, the real-time and deployment-oriented claims would benefit from a more detailed runtime analysis. Reporting only average FPS is likely insufficient when the method includes heavier Correct and Reset actions. It would help to clarify the latency associated with each action type, the frequency of these actions during inference, and whether occasional correction steps introduce problematic latency spikes. In addition, the rebuttal should address the stability of the anchored-memory design. Reviewers raised concerns about whether treating “System 2” outputs as persistent anchors could create long-term error accumulation when the detector is wrong, and whether camera ego-motion may undermine the validity of persistent anchors in endoscopic videos. Even if these issues are already implicitly handled by the architecture, they should be explained more explicitly and convincingly. Finally, the reviewers also noted some issues related to positioning and completeness, including limited discussion of prior work on memory drift and memory management in long surgical video segmentation, the need to clarify rare-class optimization in baselines, and several minor presentation issues. Overall, the paper remains competitive, but the rebuttal should focus on demonstrating that the observed gains are genuinely attributable to the proposed method, that the RL component is necessary beyond simple heuristics, and that the evaluation and deployment claims are both fair and sufficiently substantiated. | The authors’ rebuttal includes excessive new experimental results, which is a direct violation of the rebuttal guidelines. As the guidelines state, such a violation should lead to rejection. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The responses addressed the main concerns about fairness issue of evaluation setting and baselines. Yet, new results on new dataset should not be added. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers generally consider the paper clinically meaningful and technically promising, and they also recognize the value of the dataset contribution. The rebuttal clarified several concerns regarding memory stability and parts of the evaluation protocol. Although there are some concerns are partially solve, considering the reviews and response the paper is slightly above the acceptance threshold.

author_feedback: We thank all the reviewers for their time and feedback. Some expressions and paragraphs will be modified in the camera-ready. Here, we clarify the main issues raised by the reviewers. C1.To R1/R2 on suture thickness, centerline accuracy and threshold sensitivity. The qualitative blurring reflects predictive uncertainty increasing with mask area, significant at 60% but acceptable at 10%, but real-world instrument self-occlusion rarely reaches 60%. Regarding the Precision metric, ours maintains a performance gap of less than 3% compared to AOT-GAN under mask ratios of 10% and 30%. We designed the 60% mask ratios to demonstrate the robustness under extreme conditions. Our <0.5-pixel calibration error has negligible impact on performance. The clDice metric, targeting centerline accuracy, further confirms skeleton fidelity: we lead or tie all baselines and match THread (a topology-specialized method) at 10% occlusion. For uniform tubular targets manipulation in robotics, we emphasize that topological consistency outweighs exact boundary precision, since uniform thickness can be trivially recoverable from the centerline with the width prior via post-processing. On thresholds, each method has been tuned to its own optimum (ODS-style) to ensure fair comparison. Following the order in Table 1, the AP scores at 30% occlusion are 0.55, 0.44, 0.80, and 0.83(ours), respectively. Generative baselines are threshold-insensitive, their errors arise from incorrect generated geometry instead of the threshold choices. Small threshold variations do not affect our contributions on connectivity, particularly on clDice. C2.To R1/R3 on the vanilla baseline and fair comparison. The vanilla baseline shares the same architecture as ours, and implement the same two-stage training strategy, with only the pose-guided encoding removed (RoPE retained). Pretraining is essential for mitigating Transformer overfitting on the limited amount of surgical dataset. We pretrained on the Realestate dataset with a batch size of 4 for 35 epochs. Other baselines are CNN or task-specific architectures without requirements of large dataset pretraining. We verified that pretraining them before fine-tuning yields no meaningful gain over direct surgical-domain training. Consequently the reported results are fair. C3.To R3 on technical difference with PRoPE. We cite PRoPE as inspiration for combining projective relations with RoPE in attention, differences are on formulation-level: (i) PRoPE uses symmetric self-attention where every token plays an homogeneous role. Differently, we explicitly separate the occluded query view (D_o) from wrist key/value views(D_w) to model the directional relation between them, composing an asymmetric operator D_o^T D_w^(-1) suited for occlusion completion. (ii) Note also that our output transformation in Eq.1 uses D_w (wrist-side) rather than the query-side used in PRoPE to maintain numerical stability and frame consistency of the aggregated features under asymmetric setup. (iii) We transfer to a new embodied setting and emphasize that camera pose can serve as a guiding prior for embodied surgical perception, that we hope draws greater attention. C4.To R2 on proactive masking vs. real instrument occlusion. Specular reflections and depth-of-field blur can be treated as occlusion variants, degraded regions are simply masked and reconstructed via the same pipeline. Although we do not implement real-world instrument occlusion, our large-area feature-level masks pose a more challenging case, supporting the framework’s potential for severe occlusion recovery in clinical scenes. C5.To R1 on dataset acquisition and multi-wrist-view setup. Wrist-view data is captured via the robot’s dual arms recording static-scene videos, ensuring consistent targets within each sequence. Views beyond two are obtained by sampling temporally distant frames with large viewpoint displacement from the same stream, simulating multi-view images of the same scene.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes a method for semantic segmentation of thin suturing thread occlusions from multiple wrist-mounted cameras on a surgical robot. Due to the very specialised set-up, a dataset with groundtruth labels is curated as part of the paper contribution. The method is evaluated in comparison to baselines aimed at inpainting occlusions. Reviewers acknowledge that the method is methodologically sound and that the generated dataset is valuable. A few issues are identified: R1, R2 note that the proposed method over-segments the needle threads in comparison to some of the baselines. This raises questions on how much the parameters of all these methods can be tweaked to over/under segment and influence quantitative metrics. In addition, I would also like ask whether the present fixed evaluation metrics based on final predictions with predefined thresholds are enough to validate the method (this is perhaps the main parameter influencing oversegmentation). Should alternative metrics also be reported that may be less sensitive to individual method’s choice of prediction threshold? For example in edge detection literature it’s common to report metrics with data-adjusted thresholds (OIS,ODS) or that aggregate results from different thresholds (AP). R3 notes that experiment fairness needs to be clarified with further training details about the baselines R3 requests clarification regarding technical novelty of this paper compared to [4] R2 asks whether the generated dataset has enough realism to be representative of real surgery conditions and R1 requires clarifications on how the results from Fig. 4 are generated. All the above issues are appropriate to respond in a rebuttal for a more informed final decision on this paper | The authors have carefully answered to the reviewer concerns, and there is now consensus to accept this paper. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal effectively addressed the reviewers’ concerns, providing sufficient clarification and additional evidence where requested. Following the rebuttal, all reviewers expressed support for acceptance, indicating a clear consensus that the paper meets the standard for acceptance at MICCAI. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Remaining issues include over-segmentation and related choice of metric, experimental fairness, technical novelty, and dataset realism. All post-rebuttal reviews commend the author’s response, saying that the rebuttal addresses the concerns, and recommend acceptance.
